meta.title: Who really said "Jump Off the Cliff and Build Your Wings on the Way Down"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Ray Bradbury said it, not Annie Dillard. A 2005 Australian newspaper mis-credited her, and Dillard told Quote Investigator she never said or wrote it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Jump Off the Cliff and Build Your Wings on the Way Down'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Annie Dillard — Ray Bradbury. Traced to a 1979 Los Angeles Times review and a 1990 interview; Dillard denied it in writing in 2015.

answer.label: Not Annie Dillard — actually Ray Bradbury
answer.authorDates: 1920–2012 · American author of Fahrenheit 451 and The Martian Chronicles
answer.sourceLine: The cliff-and-wings image is Ray Bradbury’s, and he used it for decades: in a Los Angeles Times book review of 18 November 1979, in a 1986 keynote at UC Irvine, in an essay he wrote for Disney in 1988, and — closest to the wording people quote — in a New York Times News Service interview published 14 October 1990: “You’ve got to jump off the cliff all the time and build your wings on the way down.” Annie Dillard’s name got attached in 2005, when a Brisbane newspaper reprinted almost that exact passage under her byline; in 2015 she wrote to Quote Investigator ↗ to say plainly that she never said it or wrote it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

source.excerpt: Well, that’s nonsense. You’re going to miss life. You’ve got to jump off the cliff all the time and build your wings on the way down.
trail: November 1979 — the first citation in Quote Investigator’s trace ↗ is a Los Angeles Times book review by Bradbury himself, dated 18 November 1979, in which humanity marches from the rim of the cave to the edge of the cliff, flings itself off, and builds its wings on the way down.

1986–1990 — he says it out loud and in his own prose: a keynote at a ‘Future Style’ symposium at UC Irvine, reported in the Los Angeles Times of 21 October 1986; an essay written for Disney’s Mickey Is Sixty! in 1988, later revised for his collection Yestermorrow (1991) ↗; and the New York Times News Service interview of 14 October 1990 — all documented and footnoted by QI ↗. Wikiquote ↗ adds a fourth phrasing, cited to the Brown Daily Herald of 24 March 1995.

November 1990 — an Associated Press condensation of that interview goes out over the wires, printed in the Trenton Evening Times of 27 November 1990 in slightly smoothed form: “You’ve got to jump off cliffs all the time and build your wings on the way down” (QI ↗). This wire version, not the interview itself, is the one that later surfaces under someone else’s name.

2003 and 2005 — the line slips its moorings. A Charleston, South Carolina paper hands it to Kurt Vonnegut in August 2003; on 2 July 2005 The Courier Mail in Brisbane prints the AP wording — “jump off cliffs all the time” — under Annie Dillard’s name (QI ↗).
October 2015 — Dillard settles it herself, emailing Quote Investigator: “I never said it, or wrote it.” ↗ Her Wikiquote page ↗ carries no version of the line at all.
source.excerptNote: Bradbury’s answer in a New York Times News Service interview published 14 October 1990, in a passage arguing that pure intellect talks you out of love affairs, friendships and ventures. These are the words a Brisbane newspaper reprinted almost verbatim in 2005 — under Annie Dillard’s name (Quote Investigator ↗).

author.name: Ray Bradbury
author.heading: Ray Bradbury
author.bio: Ray Bradbury wrote The Martian Chronicles (1950) and Fahrenheit 451 (1953), and spent six decades arguing that imagination is a practical faculty rather than a decorative one. The cliff-and-wings image was one of his standing metaphors for that argument: he put it in a book review, a university keynote, an essay for Disney and more than one interview. He never fixed it as a single sentence — which is precisely why so many slightly different versions, and so many wrong names, are in circulation.

copyAttribution: "Jump off the cliff and build your wings on the way down" is Ray Bradbury, not Annie Dillard. Bradbury used the image from a Los Angeles Times book review of 18 November 1979 onward; his closest wording appears in a New York Times News Service interview published 14 October 1990: "You've got to jump off the cliff all the time and build your wings on the way down." An Australian newspaper printed almost those exact words under Annie Dillard's name in July 2005; Dillard emailed Quote Investigator in October 2015: "I never said it, or wrote it." — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a well-travelled line with three famous names on it and only one owner. Quote Investigator worked through the whole trail and, unusually, got a written answer from the author most often mis-credited.

items.why: The Courier Mail in Brisbane ran the passage under her name on 2 July 2005, in an article about taking risks; the words were those of the Associated Press condensation of Bradbury’s October 1990 interview, on the wires since that November. On 10 October 2015 Dillard emailed Quote Investigator directly — a message her literary agent confirmed later that month — to say she never said it and never wrote it (Quote Investigator ↗).

A Charleston, South Carolina paper printed “We have to continually be jumping off cliffs and developing our wings on the way down” over Vonnegut’s name on 21 August 2003. QI reports finding the adage in neither his writings nor his interviews (Quote Investigator ↗).

An airline executive told the Sunday Times in January 1998 that he lived by the rule “jump out of the plane and build your wings on the way”; the LinkedIn co-founder’s entrepreneurship version — jumping off a cliff and assembling a plane on the way down — is the one that prompted QI’s investigation in 2012 (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: Nobody said it in quite these words
items.why: The bare imperative — “Jump off the cliff and build your wings on the way down” — does not appear in that exact form in any of the Bradbury sources QI documents. In his own words it runs “You’ve got to jump off the cliff all the time…” (the interview of 14 October 1990) and “Go to the edge of the cliff and jump off. Build your wings on the way down” (Wikiquote ↗, citing the Brown Daily Herald, 24 March 1995). A 1988 sales book — Larry Wilson’s Changing the Game: The New Way to Sell, p. 156 — attributes to him “First you jump off the cliff and you build your wings on the way down”, an ascription QI records but does not trace to any Bradbury text or interview. QI notes he phrased the sentiment in more than one way; the slogan is a tidying-up of several.

misattribution.truthLine: The image, and every documented wording of it, belongs to Ray Bradbury — in print from November 1979 and repeated in essays and interviews for the next two decades (Quote Investigator ↗). Annie Dillard’s only connection to it is a newspaper error she took the trouble to correct in writing.

context.heading: Why this one is worth getting right
lead: Most misattributions die in the dark: the wrongly-credited author is long gone, or never notices, and the line keeps circulating. This one is different. Annie Dillard is alive, read the research, and wrote to the researcher — and her denial now sits in the footnotes of the very page that traces the quote. That is about as close to settled as quote provenance ever gets.

It is also a clean case study in how these things happen. There is no clever forgery here and no malice: a Brisbane feature writer’s 2005 column simply carried the passage under Dillard’s name, and the wording it used tracks the Associated Press condensation of Bradbury’s 1990 interview that had been in circulation since that November. How the name got swapped, nobody has established. Once a quotation appears in a newspaper with a Pulitzer winner’s name attached, it is effectively laundered, and it circulates for years on that authority alone.
detailsBody: Bradbury was a talker, not a slogan-writer, and he never fixed this thought in a single sentence. The version most reproduced on posters and mugs — the bare imperative — is a compression of at least four different phrasings he used between 1979 and 1995. If you want a wording you can actually cite, use the October 1990 interview or the Disney essay he revised for Yestermorrow (1991) — both are Bradbury’s own. The version that circulates from a 1988 sales book is a secondhand ascription, not a Bradbury text.

The Vonnegut version, with “developing” rather than “building” the wings, is a separate branch of the same drift. It has been circulating since at least 2003, and Quote Investigator found no trace of it in anything Vonnegut wrote or said.
context.pull: Dillard did not merely fail to say it. She wrote to the researchers to say so.

sourcesVerified.claim: Ray Bradbury is the originator; the trace runs from an 18 November 1979 Los Angeles Times book review through a 21 October 1986 UC Irvine keynote, a 1988 book quoting him, his own 1988 Disney essay reprinted in Yestermorrow (1991), and a 14 October 1990 New York Times News Service interview. Kurt Vonnegut was credited by a South Carolina paper on 21 August 2003 with no supporting evidence; The Courier Mail (Brisbane) credited Annie Dillard on 2 July 2005 with wording almost identical to Bradbury's 1990 interview; Dillard emailed QI on 10 October 2015 saying 'I never said it, or wrote it', confirmed via her agent Rob McQuilkin on 30 October 2015.

Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section for Ray Bradbury contains 'Go to the edge of the cliff and jump off. Build your wings on the way down.' cited to the Brown Daily Herald, 24 March 1995, and also quotes a 2 August 2010 CNN piece by John Blake in which Bradbury says 'I jump off the cliff and build my wings on the way down.' Life dates given as 22 August 1920 to 5 June 2012.

Wikiquote's Annie Dillard page contains no version of the cliff-and-wings line (zero occurrences of 'wings on the way down' or 'cliff' in the raw wikitext) and has no Misattributed or Disputed section; its only sections are Quotes, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, and External links.

The Internet Archive holds a scanned copy of Yestermorrow, creator Ray Bradbury, dated 1991, publisher Joshua Odell Editions (identifier isbn_9718777410861), matching the edition Quote Investigator cites for Bradbury's revised Disney essay. The item is lending-restricted, so page 141 was not independently read.
Ray Bradbury was an American writer, born 22 August 1920 and died 5 June 2012, best known for The Martian Chronicles (1950) and Fahrenheit 451 (1953).
Annie Dillard is an American author born 30 April 1945 who won the 1975 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, published in 1974.
